We study style-conditioned abstract generation from a few example abstracts per author and propose three methods: (1) contrastive activation steering, (2) a network that predicts steering vectors, and (3) a hypernetwork that predicts LoRA adapters. We find a consistent trade-off between style imitation and output quality: fine-tuning buys most of the available style signal but forfeits fluency, while the hypernetwork achieves the best trade-off on both seen and unseen authors. Our steering operates at author level, contrasting an author’s abstracts against style-neutral generations for the same content. This holds topic fixed, removes the need for a predefined style inventory, and outperforms inventory-based steering. Moreover, our analyses demonstrate that manually extracted and predicted steering vectors are near-orthogonal yet score comparably, indicating that style conditioning here can admit at least two unrelated directions rather than requiring one particular axis. 1 Introduction By in-context learning ( Brown et al., 2020 ) , large language models can solve a wide range of tasks by conditioning on a few demonstrations without parameter updates. Author-level style control, however, is not reliably one of these tasks. While coarse style attributes such as sentiment or emotion can be controlled through activation-level interventions ( Subramani et al., 2022 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Konen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , imitating an individual author from a handful of texts is harder: Horvitz et al. (2024) find that an 800M model fine-tuned on authorship embeddings outperforms GPT-4 at few-shot transfer toward specific users. This is the cold-start setting of user-level personalization ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) : per-user fine-tuning ( Tan et al., 2024c ; Dan et al., 2025 ) requires a history the new author does not have, retrieval over that history is equally unavailable ( Salemi et al., 2024 ; Richardson et al., 2023 ) , and a few examples are often insufficient for the model to extract style ( Reif et al., 2022 ; Patel et al., 2022 ) . Scientific writing exacerbates the difficulty. Formal conventions leave little surface variation, and authors write in their style about their topics, so a model extracting an author’s style risks copying content rather than form ( Wegmann et al., 2022 ; Patel et al., 2025 ) . Existing approaches address parts of this problem but leave a clear gap. Activation steering has been evaluated on coarse stylistic distinctions ( Konen et al., 2024 ) or in settings with substantial per-attribute supervision ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2024a ) , and StyleVector ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) computes and stores one contrastive vector per user offline. Adapters generated by hypernetworks ( Ha et al., 2016 ) remove per-user training, but Text-to-LoRA ( Charakorn et al., 2025 ) conditions on natural-language task descriptions, and p2p ( Tan et al., 2026 ) on user profiles assembled from history summaries and retrieval. None of these works targets fine-grained, author-level style in a strict few-shot regime. We study style-conditioned abstract generation from three example abstracts per author, comparing three baselines (zero-shot, few-shot, LoRA) against three proposed methods (§ 4 ): 1) contrastive activation steering, 2) a network predicting steering vectors, and 3) a hypernetwork predicting LoRA adapters. Our contributions are: • We expose a consistent trade-off between style imitation and output quality across all six methods, on which the hypernetwork appears to occupy the most efficient position (§ 6.4 ). • We show that manually computed and predicted steering vectors are near-orthogonal yet yield comparable style accuracy, so at least two unrelated directions support style conditioning and no particular axis is required (§ 7.1 ). • We adapt contrastive steering to the author level by contrasting ground-truth abstracts against style-neutral model generations for the same content, and find it matches or exceeds the method of Konen et al. (2024) (§ 7.2 ). 2 Related Work Few-Shot Personalization of LLMs Style-conditioned generation sits at the intersection of text style transfer and user-level personalization ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) . Horvitz et al. (2024) target the low-data regime by conditioning a small model on authorship embeddings for few-shot transfer toward individual users. The strongest personalization results, however, come from per-user fine-tuning that trains dedicated LoRA adapters ( Hu et al., 2022 ) for each user ( Tan et al., 2024c ; Tan et al., 2024b ; Dan et al., 2025 ) . This scales poorly in the number of users and degrades when user histories are limited. This work targets the cold-start setting at author-level granularity, in scientific writing, a domain whose formal constraints leave comparatively little surface variation to exploit. Activation Steering Hidden activations contain latent directions that control stylistic attributes ( Subramani et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Konen et al. (2024) derive style vectors by contrasting mean activations of a target style against a fixed set of remaining styles, at a coarse granularity such as modern versus old English. We instead contrast an author’s ground-truth abstracts against style-neutral abstracts the model generates for the same content, which removes the need for a predefined inventory, holds topic constant, and operates at author level. The matched-content contrast is close in spirit to Zhang et al. (2025b) ; our contribution is its use at author level in scientific writing and, primarily, the prediction of author-specific interventions from three examples. Zhang et al. (2025b) store one contrastive vector per user, computed offline from that user’s texts. We further train a network to predict steering vectors in a single forward pass from three examples, so no per-user artifact is computed or stored. Hypernetwork-Generated Adapters Hypernetworks Ha et al. (2016) generate adaptation parameters directly, removing the need for per-user training: prior work produces attribute-conditioned prefixes for a frozen LM ( Clive et al., 2022 ) and user-specific LoRA adapters for perspectivist classification ( Ignatev et al., 2025 ) . Text-to-LoRA ( Charakorn et al., 2025 ) , whose backbone we adopt, maps a natural-language task description to LoRA weights for zero-shot adaptation to unseen tasks. We instead predict style-conditioned adapters for a fixed task from an aggregated embedding of examples. Closest to our setting, Tan et al. (2026) map an encoded user profile to LoRA weights for long-form generation, but rely on an LLM-generated history summary and a retrieval pipeline, whereas we condition on three abstracts alone. 3 Task and Evaluation R a R_{a} frozen embedder projection + + mean 𝐳 a \mathbf{z}_{a} MLP backbone E layer ​ [ l ] E_{\mathrm{layer}}[l] E module ​ [ m ] E_{\mathrm{module}}[m] steering head LoRA head 𝐯 ( l ) \mathbf{v}^{(l)} 𝐀 ( l ) , 𝐁 ( l ) \mathbf{A}^{(l)},\mathbf{B}^{(l)} frozen LLM layer l ∈ L l\in L y ^ \hat{y} inference ℒ CE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} on abstract y y (teacher forced, prompt masked) training gradient paper outline s s r 1 , r 2 , r 3 r_{1},r_{2},r_{3} not in context Figure 1: Both style control networks differ only in their output head. Task Formulation Given a target author a a , a reference set R a = { r 1 , r 2 , r 3 } R_{a}=\{r_{1},r_{2},r_{3}\} of three abstracts by a a , and a structured outline s s of an unseen paper, the task is to generate an abstract y ^ = M ⁡ ( s , R a ) \hat{y}=M(s,R_{a}) that describes s s in the style of a a . Outlines are produced from the paper’s L a T e X source (§ 5.1 ); no model observes the original abstract as input. The base model M M is frozen throughout, and no method requires per-author training at deployment. The small size of R a R_{a} is a property of the cold-start setting ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) rather than a hyperparameter. Unlike prior work, we assume neither a rich user profile nor a retrieval corpus ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . We evaluate on authors seen during training and on held-out authors entirely (§ 5.1 ). Author Style Evaluation We measure style by authorship attribution. Instead of a standard classifier which fixes the label set at training time, our unseen-author regime requires attributing text to new authors introduced at inference from three examples. Therefore, we adopt k k -NN retrieval in a learned embedding space, which admits new authors without retraining. Specifically, an encoder is first fine-tuned on authorship classification. Then we discard its head, and create document embeddings by mean-pooling With the example abstracts forming the reference database, a query is assigned the majority label among its k k nearest neighbors under cosine distance, falling back to the nearest neighbor when no majority exists. We report accuracy and mean reciprocal rank (MRR), the latter being continuous and therefore less sensitive to sampling variance. Note that style and content are not fully separable in this metric, as abstracts generated without author information are attributed well above chance (§ 6.1 ), a known issue of authorship representations ( Wegmann et al., 2022 ; Huertas-Tato et al., 2024 ) . So we only use style accuracy to compare models rather than as an absolute metric. Topic Preservation Evaluation The generated abstracts must not deviate from the main text’s topic. Therefore, we detect off-topic generation with a binary LLM-judge. GPT-OSS-20B OpenAI (2025) receives an abstract and the introduction of a paper and decides whether both originate from the same document (prompt in Appendix A.1 ). Text Quality Evaluation Besides topic preservation, we evaluate the intrinsic quality of the generated abstracts. Perplexity is an established metric for text fluency ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) but is untrustworthy here, as it rewards the predictable, repetitive text that aggressive style conditioning may produce. Instead, we measure quality by pairwise preference by letting GPT-OSS-20B compare each generated abstract against the author’s real abstract for the same paper (prompt in Appendix A.2 ). Each pair is judged twice in swapped order to cancel position bias ( Ko et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2024 ) . We report the preference rate against the human-written abstract. Since our corpus predates 2022 when LLM-assisted writing emerged (§ 5.1 ) and the judge tends to favor LLM-generated content ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , preference rates are high across all models. However, note that it is the differences between the preference rates, not their absolute level, that carry the information. 4 Style Control Methods Manual Contrastive Steering Hidden activations contain directions that control stylistic attributes, and adding a style vector to selected layers steers generation toward the corresponding style. Prior work ( Konen et al., 2024 ) obtains the steering vector by contrasting a target style against the mean activation of all other styles in a fixed inventory. This does not transfer to our case, as such an inventory hardly exists in practice, and contrasting one author against others writing about different topics leaves content in the vector. Instead, we contrast each reference abstract against the model’s own “neutral” abstract for the same paper, generated zero-shot from s i s_{i} in the model’s default style. Specifically, for layer l l , the steering vector is 𝐯 a ( l ) = 𝐚 ¯ auth ( l ) − 𝐚 ¯ gen ( l ) , \mathbf{v}_{a}^{(l)}=\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{auth}}^{(l)}-\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{gen}}^{(l)}, (1) where both terms are activations mean-aggregated over tokens. The three per-reference vectors are averaged and injected during generation, 𝐚 steered ( l ) ​ ( x ) = 𝐚 ( l ) ​ ( x ) + λ ​ 𝐯 a ( l ) , \mathbf{a}_{\text{steered}}^{(l)}(x)=\mathbf{a}^{(l)}(x)+\lambda\,\mathbf{v}_{a}^{(l)}, (2) with intensity λ \lambda and target layers L L selected on validation (§ 5.3 ). Our approach outperforms the inventory-based method of Konen et al. (2024) , as shown in § 7.2 . Three constraints remain. First, the contrast requires one neutral generation per reference, which in turn requires the outline of the corresponding reference paper. Manual steering therefore consumes strictly more than R a R_{a} and does not satisfy the deployment setting of § 3 ; we report it not as a competing method under that setting, but as a reference point the two learned methods must match using the three abstracts alone. Second, it requires a λ \lambda search per setting: we sweep λ ∈ ⟨ grid ⟩ \lambda\in\langle\text{grid}\rangle on validation and select λ = 0.875 \lambda=0.875 for the test configuration, whereas the layer comparison in Table 5 was run at λ = 1.0 \lambda=1.0 before this search. Third, the intervention is applied to the residual stream at the ⟨ \langle output of each target block / post-attention position ⟩ \rangle during both prefill and autoregressive decoding, and the activations in Equation 1 are mean-pooled over the ⟨ \langle abstract tokens only, with prompt tokens excluded ⟩ \rangle .
